newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebels cut road to key town - officials.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels cut road to key town - officials.

text.p: Zairean rebels and their allies have taken two strategic towns, cutting government troops in the northeastern town of Bunia off from Kisangani city to the west, local officials said on Sunday.
The crossroads towns of Komanda and Mambasa, are both on the main road from Bunia to Kisangani, largest city in the region.
"We tried to reach Bunia yesterday," Kihungu Lubono Tsongo, magistrate in rebel-held Beni, told Reuters. "But (we) were turned back at Komanda...by Banyamulenge (rebel) forces."
Mustafa Lufungula, head of the Zairean Red Cross in Beni, said the Mai-Mai, a witchcraft group working for the rebels, had cut the Bunia-Kisangani road at Mambasa.
Komanda lies 60 km (35 miles) west of Bunia and Mambasa 140 km (90 miles) west. Kisangani is a further 430 km (270 miles).
Bunia -- which is reported strongly defended -- is the next target of rebels on the northern front as they extend the area they have carved out of eastern Zaire over the past seven weeks.
The Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire now controls a strip running 520 km (320 miles) north-south along Zaire's border with Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.

The rebellion has scattered at least 165,000 Rwandan refugees into the countryside of eastern Zaire. A multinational force with a mission to find and help the refugees has set up its headquarters in the Ugandan capital Kampala.
The Canadian commander of the force, Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, visited the rebel capital Goma on Sunday to seek more information on how to help refugees.

As the mission looked increasingly tenuous, a force spokesman said Baril had crossed from Rwanda to Zaire to meet rebel leader Laurent Kabila, who opposes the force deploying for fear it might restore the authority of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Kabila's military commander, Andre Kissasse Ngandu, said in an interview published on Sunday the United Nations was inflating the number of refugees still in rebel-held areas as an excuse to bring in foreign forces.
But a cabinet minister in France, which had been the main advocate of military intervention to help refugees, said in an interview published on Saturday the mission was no longer tenable.

In Beni, magistrate Tsongo said Bunia had a concentration of government troops, some pushed north by the advancing rebels and some flown in as reinforcements. This would make a garrison of about 5,000 men, the rebels said.
Tsongo said the Zairean soldiers had left a trail of destruction as they fled northwards.
On the other side of Rwanda, in northwestern Tanzania, about 1,000 Rwandan refugees walked out of two camps on Sunday, complicating U.N. plans to repatriate them.
A spokesman for the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said half the 1,000 refugees had gone off into the Tanzanian bush while the other half were apparently going home to Rwanda.
They were from the camps of Kagenyi and Rubwera, which held about 38,600 Rwandans and were part of a chain of five camps in northwestern Tanzania, he added.

Aid workers in the Tanzanian town of Ngara said it was possible some refugees feared compulsory repatriation to Rwanda, where they may face prosecution for the mass killings of minority Tutsis in 1994.
